title: Find the Letter
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
panel: Find the LetterSay each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 10).Say and look for: Say: Here are twelve letter cards from the lantern shop. I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter. Say: Point to the letter e. (top row, fourth card) Say: Point to the letter M. (top row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter a. (top row, second card) Say: Point to the letter z. (bottom row, sixth card) Say: Point to the letter K. (bottom row, first card) Say: Point to the letter q. (bottom row, fourth card) Say: Point to the letter S. (top row, first card) Say: Point to the letter j. (bottom row, second card) Say: Point to the letter T. (bottom row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter B. (top row, third card) The top row reads S, a, B, e, M, o and the bottom row reads K, j, V, q, T, z. Six cards are uppercase and six are lowercase, and two of the twelve are never asked for. This is the direction the standard asks for: the child hears a name and finds the printed letter. Keep the uppercase and the lowercase results apart in your notes. j, q and z are the letters children meet least often. If the child points to the wrong one, write down which one. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of them. A child sitting right at that goal gets about 6 of these 10, which the suggested rating reads as approaching. Count the uppercase and the lowercase separately, hold each against the number above, and set the rating yourself.

title: Uppercase Letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
panel: Uppercase LettersShow one letter at a time with the Next and Back buttons. The arrow keys work too.Keep track of each letter the student gets right, then type the number right in the box for this part.Letters: S, M, A, T, R, B, O, C, P, N, E, L, D, F, H, I, G, K, U, W, J, Y, V, Z, Q, XNotes for you: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly. Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts. Write down every letter that was missed. Which letters they are matters more than the total. If the student misses five in a row, stop this part and move on. Record what was reached. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of them. The two inventories are scored under one code, so a child right at goal lands near 33 of 52 and the suggested rating reads that as approaching. Hold the uppercase count and the lowercase count against the two numbers above and set the rating yourself.

title: First Sound Check
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the first sound.
panel: First Sound CheckSay each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 5).Say and look for: Model first: Moon. The first sound in moon is /m/. Now you try. Point to the cat. Say: Cat. What is the first sound in cat? (/k/) Point to the bird. Say: Bird. What is the first sound in bird? (/b/) Point to the hat. Say: Hat. What is the first sound in hat? (/h/) Point to the tree. Say: Tree. What is the first sound in tree? (/t/) Point to the fox. Say: Fox. What is the first sound in fox? (/f/) The answer is the sound, not the letter name. If the child says a letter name, ask: What sound do you hear first? Tree starts with two sounds run together, so /t/ is what you want.

title: Rhyme Time
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say a word that rhymes.
panel: Rhyme TimeSay each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Model first: Night, light, kite. They rhyme. They sound the same at the end. Point to the star. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with star. (car, far, jar, bar, gar) Point to the bed. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with bed. (red, fed, head, said, zed) Point to the key. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with key. (bee, see, tea, me, zee) Point to the owl. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with owl. (towel, growl, howl, dowl) Real words and silly words both count. A rhyme that is close but not perfect counts too.

title: Put It Together
dir: Listen to the slow, sleepy voice. Say the whole word.
panel: Put It TogetherRead the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Say: I am going to talk very slowly tonight. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures can help you, but they are mixed up. Say with a pause between the parts: lan ... tern. (lantern, the paper light in the first picture) Say: cab ... in. (cabin, the little wooden house in the second picture) Say the three sounds: /f/ ... /i/ ... /sh/. (fish) Say the three sounds: /b/ ... /oo/ ... /t/. (boot) The first two are syllables. The last two are single sounds. Note which kind the child can blend.

title: Rue Walks the Lantern Street
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Rue Walks the Lantern Street
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Read aloud to the student: Rue is a little fox. Rue lives at the edge of a quiet town by a river. Tonight is the first night of the new year, and the people have hung paper lanterns on a long rope over the main street. Rue wanted to see them all lit up. So Rue trotted down the sidewalk with her tail held high. First she passed the little wooden house on the corner. Next she passed the park tree, where an owl sat blinking. Then she came to the bridge over the river. (Stop here. Ask what Rue will do next.) Rue walked out to the middle of the bridge and looked down. The black water held every lantern in it. Rue sat very still and counted them twice.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This is a town at night. The people hang paper lanterns on a long rope over the street. A lantern is a little paper light you can hang up. The animal at the left is a fox. Point out the owl in the tree. Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Rue comes to the bridge. Ask at the stopping place: What do you think Rue will do next? (Any guess that fits the story, like walk onto the bridge, look at the water, cross the river, or sit down and watch.) Then read the rest. Ask: Who is this story about? What kind of animal is she? (Rue. A little fox.) Ask: Rue passed three things. What did she pass first? Next? Last? (First the little wooden house, next the park tree, last the bridge.) Count it correct when all three are in the right order. Ask: What did Rue see in the water? What did she do then? (All the lanterns, held in the black water. She sat very still and counted them twice.) If picture supports are on, the picture on the screen can help the child remember. The picture shows the fox, the house, the tree with the owl, and the bridge over the river.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Find the Letter
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
panel: Say each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 5).Say and look for: Say: Every lantern has a tag with a small letter on it. I will say a letter name. Point to the lantern with that letter. Say: Point to the letter l. (fourth lantern from the left) Say: Point to the letter s. (last lantern on the right) Say: Point to the letter m. (first lantern on the left) Say: Point to the letter t. (fifth lantern from the left) Say: Point to the letter h. (third lantern from the left) The tags read m, n, h, l, t, s from left to right. This is the other direction from the lantern tag deck: here the child hears the name and finds the printed letter. m and n look alike, and so do l and t. If the child points to the wrong one of a pair, write down which one. This stop and Find the Letter in stop 1 are scored under the same code, so their counts add together. The TK goal is a count of letters, about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase, and a child sitting right at that goal lands near 60 percent of any sample. Set the rating yourself against those two counts rather than taking the suggested one.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Why the Sky Gets Dark
dir: Listen to your teacher read about day and night. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the text marked "Read aloud to the student" below at a steady pace. Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: The sun gives us light. The earth we live on is round like a ball, and it turns around slowly all the time. When your side of the earth turns toward the sun, it is day where you are. When your side turns away from the sun, it is night, and that is when you can see the stars. The stars are up in the sky all day long too. But in the day the sun is so bright that the stars do not show.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the picture first. Say: The big round thing is the earth. That is what we live on. The sun is over here on the left. The side of the earth turned toward the sun is in the light, so it is day there. The other side is turned away, so it is dark there and it is night. Then read the facts out loud. Ask: The earth keeps turning all night long. So what will happen in the morning? (Your side will turn back toward the sun, and it will be day again. The text does not say this part, so the child has to put two facts together.) Ask: It gets dark at your house too. What do you do or turn on when it gets dark? (Uses what the child already knows: turn on a lamp, flip the light switch, use a flashlight, close the curtains. Any real answer from the child's own night counts.) Say: What do you want to know about the sky at night? Ask me a question. You can start with What, Where, or Why. (Asks a real question about the sky, the stars, the moon, or the dark. Telling a fact instead of asking is not a question.)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Write the Night Sounds
dir: Listen for the sound. Write the letter on your paper and hold it up.
panel: The student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Ask the student to hold their paper up to the camera so you can see the working, not only the answer.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Point to the first picture. Say: This is a lantern. Lantern starts with /l/. Write the letter that makes the /l/ sound. Hold it up. (l or L) Point to the moon. Say: Moon starts with /m/. Write the letter for /m/. (m or M) Point to the bowl. Say: This is soup. Soup starts with /s/. Write the letter for /s/. (s or S) Point to the last picture. Say: This is a pine tree. Pine starts with /p/. Write the letter for /p/. (p or P) A letter counts when you can tell what it is. Backward or wobbly letters still count. Uppercase or lowercase is fine. You give the word and the sound. The child picks and writes the letter. If an adult names the letter for the child, do not count that one.Then fill in the counts below.

title: The Phone Call
dir: Your teacher is calling you. Ask questions until you know what to do.
panel: Read the directions aloud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Say: You are at home in the town. I will call you on the phone, but part of my message will be missing. Ask me questions until you know what to do. Message 1. Say in a phone voice: Hello! Please bring the lantern down to the bridge. Look for: asks a question about which lantern or which bridge (there are lots of lanterns and two bridges). If the child does not ask, prompt once: Do you know which one I mean? Then answer: The gold lantern. The little bridge by the park. Message 2. Say: We start hanging them up tonight. Bring enough for the whole rope. Look for: asks a question about how many, like How many lanterns? or How long is the rope? Then answer: Bring ten lanterns. Look for: a follow-up question that builds on your answer, like Do I need a ladder too? or What time should I come? Answer it in a few words. Look for: says the plan back to you to make sure, like So the gold lantern and ten of them? If the child does not, ask: Can you tell me back what you will do? Count this check correct when the repeat is right and the child checks it with you. Count a check only when the child asks or confirms. An answer with no question does not count here.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Mystery Basket
dir: Something is in the basket on the bridge. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
panel: Mystery BasketRead the directions aloud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Your secret: a key is in the basket. Do not tell. Say: One thing is packed in this basket. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: Is it alive? What do you do with it? Answer each question in a few words: It is not alive. It is small and hard and cold. It is made of metal. It fits in your hand. You put it in a door. You turn it, and then the door opens. Look for: asks a real question to get information (not only a guess, like A lantern!). Look for: asks a follow-up question that builds on your answer (after It is made of metal, asks Is it shiny? or What is it for?). Look for: checks the idea with a question at the end (Is it a key?). If the child is stuck after 4 or 5 questions, give one more clue.

title: Name the Night Things
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.
panel: Name the Night ThingsRead the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Picture 1. Say: What is this? (a lantern, a lamp, or a light. All three count.) Picture 2. Say: What is this? (a bridge) Picture 3. Say: You look through this tube with one eye to make far away things look close, like the moon. What is it called? (a telescope. This is a harder word. Accept telescope only.) Picture 4. Say: What is this person doing? (cooking, baking, or stirring) Picture 5. Say: What is this person doing? (painting) Picture 6. Say: This is an owl. Tell me two words about what an owl is like. (Describing words such as brown, soft, round, quiet, big eyed, little, awake at night.) Pictures 1 to 3 are naming words, 4 and 5 are action words, and 6 is describing words. Note which kind was hard.

title: Bridge or Street
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.
panel: Bridge or StreetRead the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Say: Tonight you can watch the new year start from the middle of the bridge, with the whole river under you, or you can walk all the way down the lantern street, right under the lights. Which one would you pick? Tell me why. Look for: tells an opinion (picks one). Look for: gives a reason that explains the pick. If there is no reason, ask once: Why? Say: Tell me more about your night. What would you see? What would it feel like? Look for: 2 or more details in the description. Say: It is dark out and it is cold. What will you take with you? Tell me your plan. Look for: an explanation that makes sense, like take a coat, hold a lantern, or bring a blanket to sit on.

title: Label the New Year Page
dir: Draw one thing you want to try this year. Write letters to tell what it is. Hold it up.
panel: The student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Ask the student to hold their paper up to the camera so you can see the working, not only the answer.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Say: A new year is a fresh start. Draw one thing you want to try this year. Then write a word or some letters to tell what it is. Hold it up and tell me what you wrote. Look for: writing that is separate from the drawing (letters or marks that look like letters, not only a picture). Look for: 2 or more letters you can recognize. They do not need to spell the word. Look for: the child tells you what the writing says, like It says swim. This shows the letters stand for a word or an idea. The child can draw and label anything they want to try, like swimming, a long walk, or looking at the stars. If the child writes only a name, that is a fine start. Ask: What does it say? Then ask for some letters about the drawn thing too.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Count the Lanterns
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one over to the side as you count it out loud. (One number word for each thing moved, no skips and no double counts. Moving each object is what makes the matching visible to you, so watch the hands as well as the numbers.) Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down partway, write down the number it broke at.) Those first two counts are the evidence for this standard, because they are the ones you can see for yourself. The screen rows below are still worth doing and they show whether a count holds together over bigger groups, but the child is pointing at a monitor you cannot see, so do not rate this standard on them alone and do not rate it on what an adult in the room reports. Row 1. Say: The town hangs its lanterns up. Point to each lantern on your screen and count out loud. (10 lanterns in one line) Look for one number word for each lantern, with no skips and no double counts. Row 2. Say: Now count the stars. There are two lines of them. (12 stars, in lines of 6 and 6) Row 3. Say: Now count the little houses. (14 houses, in lines of 7 and 7) Row 4. Say: Now count the sky sparks. (11 sparks, in lines of 6 and 5) Count an item correct only when the last number said matches the number of objects. On the screen rows, have the child say the numbers slowly enough that you can hear one number word for each picture, and watch the child's eyes move along the row. Where you cannot tell, leave the row out of the count rather than taking an adult's word for it. Note where the count broke down: skipped a number, counted one twice, or lost track after 10.Then fill in the counts below.

title: More Lanterns or More Stars?
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
panel: Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Box 1. Say: Are there more lanterns or more stars? How do you know? (More lanterns. 9 lanterns and 6 stars.) Box 2. Say: Are there more houses, more trees, or the same number of each? (The same. 5 houses and 5 trees.) Box 3. Say: Which group has fewer, the owls or the stars? (Fewer owls. 3 owls and 8 stars. The owls are spread far apart, so their row looks long even though there are only 3 of them.) Box 4. Say: Which group has fewer, the lanterns or the sky sparks? (Fewer lanterns. 7 lanterns and 8 sparks. The lanterns are spread out, so their row looks longer.) Look for counting, not guessing from how long the row is. Listen for the words more, same, fewer, or less. If the child guesses from the length of the row in box 3 or box 4, say: Let's count them together, and note that the answer needed help.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Window Shapes
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw a shape on your paper.
panel: The student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student works on paper. Ask to see it when they finish.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Say: Here is a house at night, drawn with shapes. What shape is the purple roof? (triangle) Say: What shape is the blue window? (square) Say: What shape is the green door? (rectangle) Say: What shape is the yellow moon? (circle) Say: Tell me about the blue square. How many sides does it have? How many corners? (4 sides and 4 corners. Words like straight, flat, or even are a plus.) Say: Draw a square on your paper. Hold it up. (A closed shape with 4 straight sides and 4 corners. It does not need to be neat or even.)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Sort the Lanterns
dir: Look at the tray and the pile. Answer out loud.
panel: Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Point to the tray. Say: Here are the lanterns the town is about to hang up. How many lanterns are on the tray in all? (8) Say: Sort them by color in your head. How many red? How many gold? (4 red and 4 gold) Say: Now forget the color. Sort them by size. How many big? How many small? (4 big and 4 small) Say: Now two things at once. Find the lanterns that are red AND big. How many? (2) Say: Find the lanterns that are gold AND small. How many? (2) Point to the pile under the tray. Say: Put these into groups. How many groups did you make? Tell me your rule. (3 groups by what they are: 3 stars, 3 lanterns, 2 pine trees. Any rule the child can say and stick to counts, even one you did not expect.) Sorting by two things at once is the hard part. If the child can sort by color and by size but not both at once, note that: one attribute is there and two is not yet.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Tallest Pole, Longest Rope
dir: Look at the poles and the ropes. Answer out loud.
panel: Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 5).Say and look for: Point to the poles. Say: The town has five lantern poles. Which pole is the tallest? (B) Say: Which pole is the shortest? (A) Say: Now put all five poles in order, from the shortest one to the tallest one. (A, D, C, E, B) Count it correct when all five are in the right order. Point to the ropes. Say: Which rope is the longest? Which one is the shortest? (Rope 2 is the longest. Rope 4 is the shortest.) All four start at the same dotted line, so the child can compare the far ends. Say: Put all four ropes in order, from the shortest one to the longest one. (4, 1, 3, 2) Count it correct when all four are in the right order. Five in a row is harder than two. If the child can pick the tallest and the shortest but cannot order the middle three, write that down: the comparing is there and the ordering is not yet.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Where in Town?
dir: Look at the town. Answer out loud.
panel: Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Say: Here is the town at night. Look at the bridge at the other end of the street. What is on the bridge? (the gold lantern) Say: What is next to the house? (the park tree) Say: What is under the tree? (the cat) Say: Look up in the sky above the house. What is up there? (the birds. There are two.) Say: Is the bridge near the house or far from the house? (far. The bridge is way off at the other end of the street.) Say: What is between the house and the bridge? (the tree, with the cat under it) Look for a position word in the answer, not only a pointing finger. If the child only points, ask: Can you tell me with words?Then fill in the counts below.

title: Number Cards
dir: Say the name of each number.
panel: Number CardsShow one number at a time with the Next and Back buttons. The arrow keys work too.Keep track of each number the student reads correctly, then type the number right in the box for this part.Numbers, in order: 4, 9, 1, 7, 3, 10, 6, 2, 8, 5Notes for you: Say: The town wrote a number on every box of lanterns. What number is this? Click Next after each one. The deck is 4, 9, 1, 7, 3, 10, 6, 2, 8, 5. It is out of order on purpose, so the child cannot count along to find a name. Correct means the child says the number name on sight. Watch for 6 and 9 mixed up. Write down the ones missed. If the child counts up on fingers from 1 to find a name, note it. That is not the same as knowing the numeral on sight.

title: What Comes Next?
dir: Look at each row. Say what comes next.
panel: What Comes Next?Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Row 1. Say: Star, lantern, star, lantern, star, lantern, star. What comes next? (a lantern) Row 2. Say: Look at this row. What comes next? (a pine tree. The pattern is pine, pine, star, star, and the row ends with the second star.) Row 3. Say: What comes next here? (a star. The pattern is lantern, star, pine, and the row ends with a lantern.) Go back to row 1. Say: What part keeps repeating over and over? (star, lantern) Row 1 is the easy one and row 2 is the hard one, because the repeating part is four long. Note which rows worked.

title: The Town Chart
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud. Then make marks on your paper.
panel: The Town ChartThe student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student works on paper. Ask to see it when they finish.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Say: The children in town picked where they want to watch the first night of the new year, out on the bridge or down the lantern street. Each face is one child. How many children picked the bridge? (5) Say: Did more children pick the bridge or the lantern street? (The lantern street. 7 is more than 5.) Say: On your paper, make one mark for each child who picked the bridge. Hold it up. (5 marks, one for each face in the bridge row) Say: One more child picks the bridge. What should we add to the chart? (One more face in the bridge row, because each face is one child. That makes 6.)

title: Name the Letter
dir: Say the name of each letter.
panel: Name the LetterShow one letter at a time with the Next and Back buttons. The arrow keys work too.Keep track of each letter the student reads correctly, then type the number right in the box for this part.Letters, in order: L, N, C, H, P, U, F, D, W, Y, l, n, c, r, i, gNotes for you: Say: Every lantern in the town has a tag with a letter on it. Tell me the name of each letter. Click Next after each one. Correct means the child says the letter name. If the child gives the sound instead, ask once: What is the name of this letter? The first 10 are uppercase (L N C H P U F D W Y). The last 6 are lowercase (l n c r i g). Write down the ones missed. Uppercase L and lowercase l share one name, and they are the first and the eleventh card, so you can hear whether the child knows both shapes. End of TK goal: about 15 to 20 uppercase and 12 to 16 lowercase letter names. This deck is a sample of 16, so write the uppercase and lowercase results separately in your notes. These letters are not the ones used in the LP 5 game. If you have that record sheet, compare the two. If the child misses 4 in a row, stop and write down how many were tried. Find the Letter at the top of this stop is the part this standard is written for. The standard asks the child to match a spoken name to its printed form, and naming a letter on sight is harder than that, so rate this standard on the Find the Letter count and keep this deck as the extra note. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of any deck. title: Read the Story
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Juno woke before anyone else in the house. She pulled on two sweaters. Then she carried the last paper lantern down to the river. All week the crew had strung ropes across the main street. Juno had watched from the window. Tonight every lantern was lit but one. The rope sagged in the middle. So she stood on a crate to reach the empty hook. Her hands shook in the cold. She hung the lantern, stepped down, and looked up. The whole street glowed above her. Down in the black water the lights floated too. It looked as if the river had a street of its own.

title: Why Stars Twinkle
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about stars. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Why Stars Twinkle A star does not blink. Far out in space it shines with a steady light. The twinkle happens much closer to you, in the air above your head. Air is always moving. Warm air bends light a little more than cold air does. The moving air slides past. The thin beam of starlight bends this way and that. From the ground the star seems to jump and flicker. A planet looks steadier. A planet is close enough to show a tiny disk. It shows a disk instead of a single point. Astronauts above the air see stars that do not twinkle at all.
qs: What makes a star seem to twinkle?
Where does the twinkle happen?
Why does a planet look steadier than a star?
Who sees stars that do not twinkle at all?
Your turn. Ask a question about stars. Start with who, what, where, when, why, or how.

title: The Two Lanterns
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the short story. Then answer out loud.
text: The Two Lanterns A brand new lantern hung beside an old one on the rope. My paper is bright red, said the new lantern. Everyone will look at me, not at you. That night the wind came hard. The new lantern was tied with one quick knot. It slipped and hung down crooked. Its light was pointing at the ground. The old lantern was tied with three careful knots. It stayed up straight and lit the whole street until morning.
qs: Retell this story in your own words. Tell what happened first, next, and last.
What is the lesson of this story?
panel: Read the directions aloud. Then read the text on the screen aloud, once, and again if the student asks. Then read each question, one at a time.Keep track of which answers are right, then type the number right in the box for this part (out of 2).Retell this story in your own words. Tell what happened first, next, and last.Answer: The retelling has the three parts in order: the new lantern boasted about its bright red paper, the wind came hard that night, and the new lantern slipped crooked while the old one held up straight and lit the street. Two of the three, in order, is a partial retelling. All three, with details, is a complete one.What is the lesson of this story?Answer: Careful work lasts, or doing a job well matters more than looking new and bright, or do not boast. Any lesson the student can tie back to the knots or to the boasting counts. Retelling the plot again instead of naming a lesson does not.Then fill in the counts below.

Most of the water on Earth is in the ocean and it is salty. Is the water in this river salty or fresh, and how would you know?
Sort these four into solid water and liquid water: the ice along the canal edge, the water in the river, the frost on the workshop roof, the rain in the gutter.

Is the water in this river salty or fresh, and how would you know?Answer: Fresh. You can tell because people and animals drink it and crops are watered with it, and salty water would kill the plants. title: Holding the Bank, and a Map of the Town
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The river keeps eating into the bank beside the footpath. The town tried two ways to hold it and measured how much bank was lost in a year. What was put along the bank Bank lost in one year nothing 60 centimeters a facing of heavy stones 5 centimeters a row of willow stakes that grew roots 10 centimeters in the first year
qs: Which one held the bank best in that first year?
How do you know, using the numbers in the chart?
The willow roots get thicker every year and the stones stay as they are. What might the chart look like after ten years, and why?
panel: Holding the Bank, and a Map of the TownRead the directions aloud. Then read the text on the screen aloud, once, and again if the student asks. The reason must come from the numbers.The willow roots get thicker every year and the stones stay as they are. What might the chart look like after ten years, and why?Answer: The willows might hold as well as the stones or better, because their roots keep growing and spreading through the soil, while the stones do not change. Any answer that uses the idea of roots growing counts. This is a prediction, so a sensible reason matters more than the number.

text: A lantern frame is made of wire. It has 12 short pieces. It has 8 ties. One of the makers undid every tie. He laid the wire out straight. It lay on the bench.

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled

text: Two things happened in the workshop on the same evening. What happened A block of candle wax was warmed in a tin and ran into a smooth pool. A sheet of paper was left leaning on the hot lamp and went brown and brittle.
qs: Take the tin of melted wax off the heat and let it stand overnight. What happens to it?
Take the brown brittle paper away from the lamp and let it stand overnight. Does it go back to white paper?

Ask one question that would help you fix it.

title: Someone Who Made a Difference
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about him. Answer out loud.
text: Albert Einstein was a boy. He asked questions. Nobody around him could answer them. He wondered what you would see. You might ride along beside a beam of light. He did not do well at some schools. They wanted him to repeat things back. After university he could only get one job. It was checking papers. He worked in a patent office. He kept thinking in his spare time. He wrote his ideas down. They changed what everyone understood. It was about light, time and space. Later he moved to the United States. He taught at a university. He spoke up for peace. He spoke up for people being treated fairly.
qs: What kind of question did Albert Einstein wonder about as a boy?

title: Find the Letter
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
panel: Find the LetterSay each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 10).Say and look for: Say: Here are twelve letter cards from the kindness jar. I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter. Say: Point to the letter q. (top row, fourth card) Say: Point to the letter N. (top row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter h. (top row, second card) Say: Point to the letter c. (bottom row, sixth card) Say: Point to the letter P. (bottom row, first card) Say: Point to the letter l. (bottom row, fourth card) Say: Point to the letter D. (top row, first card) Say: Point to the letter y. (bottom row, second card) Say: Point to the letter F. (bottom row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter G. (top row, third card) The top row reads D, h, G, q, N, t and the bottom row reads P, y, U, l, F, c. Six cards are uppercase and six are lowercase, and two of the twelve are never asked for. This is the direction the standard asks for: the child hears a name and finds the printed letter. Keep the uppercase and the lowercase results apart in your notes. l and t are both tall and thin, and q and y both hang below the line. If the child points to the wrong one of a pair, write down which one. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of them. A child sitting right at that goal gets about 6 of these 10, which the suggested rating reads as approaching. Count the uppercase and the lowercase separately, hold each against the number above, and set the rating yourself.

title: Nell's Kind Morning
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Nell's Kind Morning
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Read aloud to the student: Nell is a little rabbit. Nell lives in a burrow at the edge of a wide green meadow. On the shelf by her door she keeps a glass jar, and every time she helps somebody she drops a paper heart into it. This morning the jar had only one heart in it, and Nell wanted to fill it up. So she hopped out into the meadow to look for somebody who needed a hand. First she came to the garden, where her neighbor Bram was trying to carry a heavy watering can all by himself. Nell took the other handle and they carried it together. Next she came to the gate, where a small brown dog was stuck on the wrong side. Nell pushed the latch up and let him through. Then she came to the pond. (Stop here. Ask what Nell will do next.) A duck was swimming in slow circles with a long piece of string caught on her foot. Nell waded in and pulled the string loose, slow and gentle, so the duck would not be scared. Then Nell hopped home and dropped three paper hearts into the jar.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This is a rabbit named Nell. Here is her burrow, and here she is hopping across the meadow. Then comes a garden, then a gate, then a pond. Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Nell comes to the pond. Ask at the stopping place: What do you think Nell will do next? (Any guess that fits the story, like help the duck, pull the string off, or get in the water.) Then read the rest. Ask: Who is this story about? What kind of animal is she? (Nell. A little rabbit.) Ask: Nell came to three places. Where did she stop first? Next? Last? (First the garden, next the gate, last the pond.) Count it correct when all three are in the right order. Ask: What did Nell do at the gate? (She pushed the latch up and let the little dog through.) If picture supports are on, the picture on the screen can help the child remember. The garden, the gate, and the pond are the last three pictures, in the same order as the story. The first two pictures show Nell at home and in the meadow.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Find the Letter

title: Read the Story
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Tess was the only one still working when the light started to go. Every other row on the hill had been weeded and watered hours before. Hers was the long row at the bottom. Nobody wanted that row. The hose would not stretch that far. Every bucket had to be carried by hand. She was halfway down it when she heard the gate swing. title: How a Seed Wakes Up
dir: Listen to your teacher read about seeds. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the text marked "Read aloud to the student" below at a steady pace. Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: A seed looks small and dry on the outside. Inside it, a tiny plant is folded up and waiting. A seed needs three things to wake up. It needs soil to sit in, water to drink, and air that is warm. When the rain soaks into the soil, the seed drinks the water in and swells up until its skin splits open. A little white root comes out first and pushes down into the soil. The root holds the plant in place and drinks more water. Then a green shoot pushes up toward the light. At the top of the shoot, the first two leaves open out. From then on the plant makes its own food out of sunlight.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the picture first. (No, or probably not. A seed needs water and warm air, and the dry cold pot has neither. The facts never say this part, so the child has to put two of them together.) Say: What do you want to know about seeds? Ask me a question. You can start with What, Where, or Why. (Asks a real question about seeds, roots, water or plants. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down partway, write down the number it broke at.) The screen rows below are still worth doing and they show whether a count holds together over bigger groups, but the child is pointing at a monitor you cannot see, so do not rate this standard on them alone and do not rate it on what an adult in the room reports. title: What a Seed Needs

text: What a Seed Needs A seed is a tiny plant. It has its own lunch. The lunch is packed around it. The seed stays dry and still. It waits until three things reach it. First it needs water. A small white root pushes down.

title: Read the Story
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: On the last Saturday of the month the whole block meets. They gather at the empty lot on the corner. Somebody brings a wheelbarrow. Somebody else brings a crate of seedlings in paper cups. We pull last year's dry stalks out of the beds. We shake the soil off the roots. Then we rake the beds flat. We cut shallow trenches with the edge of a hoe. The seedlings go in a hand's width apart. We press the soil around each one. By noon the field of weeds is gone. Instead the lot is four long green rows. Then it rains, which is exactly what we wanted.

title: Why It Rains
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about rain. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Why It Rains Every day the sun warms the top of the ocean. Some of that water turns into a gas you cannot see. The gas rises with the warm air. High up, the air is cold, and the cold turns the gas back into tiny drops. Millions of those drops floating together are what you see as a cloud. The drops bump into each other and join up. A drop gets too heavy for the air to hold. Then it falls. That is rain. The same water has been going around like this for a very long time.
qs: What does the sun do to the top of the ocean?

title: The Two Rows
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Two Rows Ravi was given a packet of bean seeds. He planted them in two short rows. He watered both rows the same. But he could not stop wondering about the row by the fence. Every afternoon he dug one of those seeds up. He wanted to see how it was doing. He brushed the soil off and looked at it. Then he pushed it back in. After two weeks the first row was a line of green plants. They stood as high as his knee. The row by the fence was still bare soil. His aunt told him about seeds. A seed does its growing down in the dark. Every time he lifted it out, it had to start over. Ravi planted the fence row again. This time he kept his hands out of the soil. By the end of the month both rows were climbing their poles.
qs: Tell me this story again in your own words. What happened first, next, and last?
What did Ravi do every afternoon?

Keep the uppercase and the lowercase results apart in your notes. a, e and o are all small and round, and M and N look alike. If the child points to the wrong one of a pair, write down which one. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of them. A child sitting right at that goal gets about 6 of these 10, which the suggested rating reads as approaching. Count the uppercase and the lowercase separately, hold each against the number above, and set the rating yourself.

title: First Sound Check
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the first sound.
panel: First Sound CheckSay each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Model first: Lake. The first sound in lake is /l/. Now you try. Point to the deer. Say: Deer. What is the first sound in deer? (/d/) Point to the fish. Say: Fish. What is the first sound in fish? (/f/) Point to the soup. Say: Soup. What is the first sound in soup? (/s/) The card is a bowl of soup, so name it the soup, not the bowl. Point to the map. Say: Map. What is the first sound in map? (/m/) The answer is the sound, not the letter name. If the child says a letter name, ask: What sound do you hear first?

title: Rhyme Time
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say a word that rhymes.
panel: Rhyme TimeSay each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Model first: Camp, lamp, stamp. They rhyme. They sound the same at the end. Point to the tent. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with tent. (bent, went, sent, dent, zent) Point to the bear. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with bear. (chair, hair, pear, care, stair, zair) Point to the boot. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with boot. (root, hoot, scoot, fruit, zoot) Real words and silly words both count. A rhyme that is close but not perfect counts too.

title: Put It Together
dir: Listen to the slow, sleepy voice. Say the whole word.
panel: Put It TogetherRead the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Say: I am going to talk very slowly out here on the water. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures can help you, but they are mixed up. Say with a pause between the parts: ca ... noe. (canoe, the little boat in the first picture) Say: ot ... ter. (otter, the swimming animal in the second picture) Say the three sounds: /p/ ... /ie/ ... /n/. (pine) Say the three sounds: /h/ ... /a/ ... /t/. (hat) The first two are syllables. The last two are single sounds. Note which kind the child can blend.

title: Mira Walks to the Dock
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Mira Walks to the Dock
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Read aloud to the student: Mira woke up first at camp. The lake was flat and shiny, and the whole hill smelled like pine. Mira wanted one more log for the campfire, so she took her bucket and walked down the trail. First she passed the green tent. Next she passed the tall pine tree, where a squirrel sat with its tail curled up. Then she came to the wooden dock. (Stop here. Ask what Mira will do next.) Mira walked out to the end of the dock and sat down. A little fish came up and looked at her toes. Mira laughed. Then she picked up the log lying beside the dock and carried it all the way back to camp.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This is a camp beside a lake. A dock is a wooden walkway that goes out over the water. The girl in the picture is Mira, and she is carrying her bucket. The picture also shows the green tent, the tall pine tree with the squirrel, and the dock, the same things she walks past in the story. Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Mira comes to the dock. Ask at the stopping place: What do you think Mira will do next? (Any guess that fits the story, like walk out on the dock, sit down, or look at the water.) Then read the rest. Ask: Who is this story about? What did she want to find? (Mira. One more log for the campfire.) Ask: Mira passed three things. What did she pass first? Next? Last? (First the green tent, next the tall pine tree, last the dock.) Count it correct when all three are in the right order. Ask: What came up and looked at her toes? What did she carry back to camp? (A little fish. The log that was lying beside the dock.) If picture supports are on, the picture on the screen can help the child remember. The picture shows Mira with her bucket, the green tent, the tall pine tree with the squirrel, and the dock.Then fill in the counts below.

title: How a Pine Tree Plants Itself
dir: Listen to your teacher read about pine cones. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the text marked "Read aloud to the student" below at a steady pace. Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: A pine tree grows its seeds inside a cone. The cone is hard and brown, and all winter long it stays shut tight. When summer comes and the air turns warm and dry, the cone opens up. Little seeds slip out from under the scales and spin down to the ground. Squirrels love pine seeds. A squirrel gathers up a pile of them and buries them in small holes all over the forest floor.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the picture first. Say: This shows what happens to a pine cone, in order. Top left: the cone is shut tight in the snow. Top right: the sun is out, the cone opens, and little seeds spin out. Bottom left: a squirrel gathers a pile of the seeds. Bottom right: the squirrel buries the seeds in small holes. Then read the facts out loud. Ask: A squirrel buries more seeds than it can eat, and it does not dig up every hole again. What do you think happens to the seeds that stay in the ground? (They grow into new pine trees. The text does not say this part, so the child has to put two facts together.) Ask: Have you ever watched an animal carry food away or hide it? Tell me about it. (Uses what the child already knows: a squirrel with a nut, a bird with a crumb, a dog with a bone, an ant with a crumb. Any real answer from the child's own life counts.) Say: What do you want to know about pine trees? Ask me a question. You can start with What, Where, or Why. (Asks a real question about pine trees, cones, seeds, or the forest. Telling a fact instead of asking is not a question.)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Sound Letters
dir: Listen for the sound. Write the letter on your paper and hold it up.
panel: Sound LettersThe student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Ask the student to hold their paper up to the camera so you can see the working, not only the answer.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Point to the first picture. Say: This is a log. Log starts with /l/. Write the letter that makes the /l/ sound. Hold it up. (l or L) Point to the tent. Say: Tent starts with /t/. Write the letter for /t/. (t or T) Point to the third picture. Say: This is a pan, the one we cook in. Pan starts with /p/. Write the letter for /p/. (p or P) Point to the last picture. Say: This is a bird. Bird starts with /b/. Write the letter for /b/. (b or B) A letter counts when you can tell what it is. Backward or wobbly letters still count. Uppercase or lowercase is fine. You give the word and the sound. The child picks and writes the letter. If an adult names the letter for the child, do not count that one.

title: Label Your Pack
dir: Draw one thing you would pack for camp. Write letters to tell what it is. Hold it up.
panel: Label Your PackThe student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Ask the student to hold their paper up to the camera so you can see the working, not only the answer.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: If picture supports are on, the tent, backpack, and boots are only ideas for what to bring. The child can draw anything. Say: Draw one thing you would put in your pack for camp. Then write a word or some letters to tell what it is. Hold it up and tell me what you wrote. Look for: writing that is separate from the drawing (letters or marks that look like letters, not only a picture). Look for: 2 or more letters you can recognize. They do not need to spell the word. Look for: the child tells you what the writing says, like It says hat. This shows the letters stand for a word or an idea. If the child writes only a name, that is a fine start. Ask: What does it say? Then ask for some letters about the packed thing too.

title: Name It
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.
panel: Name ItRead the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Picture 1. Say: What is this? (a canoe or a boat. Both count.) Picture 2. Say: What is this? (a backpack, a pack, or a bag.) Picture 3. Say: You hold this in your hand and it makes a beam of light when it is dark. What is it called? (a flashlight. This is a harder word. A light or a lantern also counts.) Picture 4. Say: What is this person doing? (swimming) Picture 5. Say: What is this person doing? (running) Picture 6. Say: This is an owl. Tell me two words about what an owl is like. (Describing words such as brown, soft, round, quiet, big eyed, little, awake at night.) Pictures 1 to 3 are naming words, 4 and 5 are action words, and 6 is describing words. Note which kind was hard.

title: Mystery Pack
dir: Something is packed in the backpack. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
panel: Mystery PackRead the directions aloud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Your secret: an apple is in the pack. Do not tell. Say: One thing is packed in this backpack. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: Is it alive? What do you do with it? Answer each question in a few words: It is not alive. It fits in your hand. It is red. It is round and smooth. You can eat it. It is a fruit. It goes crunch when you bite it. Look for: asks a real question to get information (not only a guess, like A hat!). Look for: asks a follow-up question that builds on your answer (after You can eat it, asks Is it sweet? or Is it a fruit?). Look for: checks the idea with a question at the end (Is it an apple?). If the child is stuck after 4 or 5 questions, give one more clue.

title: Lake or Trail
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.
panel: Lake or TrailRead the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Say: This afternoon you can paddle the canoe out on the lake, or you can hike up the trail through the pine trees. Which one would you pick? Tell me why. Look for: tells an opinion (picks one). Look for: gives a reason that explains the pick. If there is no reason, ask once: Why? Say: Tell me more about your afternoon. What would you see out there? What would it feel like? Look for: 2 or more details in the description.

title: Count the Camp
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one over to the side as you count it out loud. (One number word for each thing moved, no skips and no double counts. Moving each object is what makes the matching visible to you, so watch the hands as well as the numbers.) Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down partway, write down the number it broke at.) Those first two counts are the evidence for this standard, because they are the ones you can see for yourself. The screen rows below are still worth doing and they show whether a count holds together over bigger groups, but the child is pointing at a monitor you cannot see, so do not rate this standard on them alone and do not rate it on what an adult in the room reports. Row 1. Say: Here is the wood pile for the campfire. Point to each log on your screen and count out loud. (11 logs in one line) Look for one number word for each log, with no skips and no double counts. Row 2. Say: Now count the acorns. There are two lines of them. (13 acorns, in lines of 7 and 6) Row 3. Say: Now count the fish. (15 fish, in lines of 8 and 7) Row 4. Say: Now count the frogs. (12 frogs, in lines of 6 and 6) Count an item correct only when the last number said matches the number of objects. On the screen rows, have the child say the numbers slowly enough that you can hear one number word for each picture, and watch the child's eyes move along the row. Where you cannot tell, leave the row out of the count rather than taking an adult's word for it. Note where the count broke down: skipped a number, counted one twice, or lost track after 10.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Number Cards
dir: Say the name of each number.
panel: Number CardsShow one number at a time with the Next and Back buttons. The arrow keys work too.Keep track of each number the student reads correctly, then type the number right in the box for this part.Numbers, in order: 6, 2, 9, 4, 1, 8, 3, 10, 5, 7Notes for you: Say: The camp counts everything. What number is this? Click Next after each one. Correct means the child says the number name. Write down the ones missed. Watch for 6 and 9 mixed up. If the child counts up on fingers to find the name, note it. The goal is to know each numeral on sight.

title: More or Fewer
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
panel: More or FewerRead the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Box 1. Say: Are there more logs or more fish? How do you know? (More logs. 7 logs and 4 fish.) Box 2. Say: Are there more tents, more canoes, or the same number of each? (The same. 5 tents and 5 canoes.) Box 3. Say: Which group has fewer, the deer or the acorns? (Fewer deer. 4 deer and 9 acorns. The deer are spread far apart and the acorns are packed close together, so the deer row reaches further across the box even though there are fewer of them.) Look for counting, not guessing from how far a row reaches. Listen for the words more, same, fewer, or less. If the child guesses from the length of the row in box 3, say: Let's count them together, and note that the answer needed help.

title: Sort the Stones
dir: Look at the tree stump and the pile. Answer out loud.
panel: Sort the StonesRead the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Point to the tree stump. Say: Here are the stones we picked up along the lake. How many stones are on the tree stump in all? (8) Say: Sort them by color in your head. How many grey? How many tan? (4 grey and 4 tan) Say: Now forget the color. Sort them by size. How many big? How many small? (4 big and 4 small) Say: Now two things at once. Find the stones that are grey AND big. How many? (2) Say: Find the stones that are tan AND small. How many? (2) Point to the pile under the tree stump. Say: Put these into groups. How many groups did you make? Tell me your rule. (3 groups by what they are: 3 acorns, 3 leaves, 2 fish. Any rule the child can say and stick to counts, even one you did not expect.) Sorting by two things at once is the hard part. If the child can sort by color and by size but not both at once, note that: one attribute is there and two is not yet.

title: Camp Chart
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud. Then make marks on your paper.
panel: Camp ChartThe student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student works on paper. Ask to see it when they finish.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Say: The children at camp picked what they like best, paddling the canoe or swimming at the dock. Each face is one child. How many children picked the canoe? (6) Say: Did more children pick the canoe or swimming? (The canoe. 6 is more than 4.) Say: On your paper, make one mark for each child who picked swimming. Hold it up. (4 marks, one for each face in the swimming row) Say: One more child picks swimming. What should we add to the chart? (One more face in the swimming row, because each face is one child. That makes 5.)

title: Name the Shapes
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw a shape on your paper.
panel: Name the ShapesThe student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student works on paper. Ask to see it when they finish.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Say: Here is the camp, drawn with shapes. What shape is the green tent? (triangle) Say: What shape is the blue window on the cabin? (square) Say: What shape is the long orange board on the front of the dock? (rectangle) Say: What shape is the yellow sun? (circle) Say: Tell me about the blue square. How many sides does it have? How many corners? (4 sides and 4 corners. Words like straight, flat, or even are a plus.) Say: Draw a triangle on your paper. Hold it up. (A closed shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners. It does not need to be neat or even.)

title: Where at Camp?
dir: Look at the camp. Answer out loud.
panel: Where at Camp?Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Say: Here is the whole camp. Look at the wooden dock. What is on the dock? (the canoe) Say: What is next to the tent? (the backpack, or the pack) Say: What is in the lake? (the fish) Say: Look up in the sky right above the tent. What is up there? (the bird) Say: What is between the tent and the dock? (the pine tree) Say: Is the mountain near the camp or far from the camp? (far. The mountain is way off behind the hills.) Look for a position word in the answer, not only a pointing finger. If the child only points, ask: Can you tell me with words?

title: Tallest Tree
dir: Look at the trees. Answer out loud.
panel: Tallest TreeRead the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Point to the trees. Say: Five pine trees grow along the camp trail. Which tree is the tallest? (B) Say: Which tree is the shortest? (A) Say: Now put all five trees in order, from the shortest one to the tallest one. (A, C, E, D, B) Count it correct when all five are in the right order. All five trees stand on the same line, so the child can compare the tops. Five in a row is harder than two. If the child can pick the tallest and the shortest but cannot order the middle three, write that down: the comparing is there and the ordering is not yet.

title: What Comes Next?
dir: Look at each row. Say what comes next.
panel: What Comes Next?Read the directions aloud.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Row 1. Say: Tent, pine, tent, pine, tent, pine, tent. What comes next? (a pine tree) Row 2. Say: Look at this row. What comes next? (a fish. The pattern is fish, fish, frog, frog, and the row ends with the second frog.) Row 3. Say: What comes next here? (a leaf. The pattern is acorn, leaf, log, and the row ends with an acorn.) Go back to row 1. Say: What part keeps repeating over and over? (tent, pine) Extra if there is time: clap and pat row 1 together (clap, pat, clap, pat). This shows the child can copy a pattern in a new way.

title: Name the Letter
dir: Say the name of each letter.
panel: Name the LetterShow one letter at a time with the Next and Back buttons. The arrow keys work too.Keep track of each letter the student reads correctly, then type the number right in the box for this part.Letters, in order: V, J, Q, Z, Y, K, T, R, B, S, v, j, q, z, y, kNotes for you: Say: Every marker on the camp trail has a letter on it. Tell me the name of each letter. Click Next after each one. Correct means the child says the letter name. If the child gives the sound instead, ask once: What is the name of this letter? The first 10 are uppercase (V J Q Z Y K T R B S). The last 6 are lowercase (v j q z y k). Each of the last 6 is the small version of one of the first 6, so you hear the same name twice and can tell which shape the child knows. Write down the ones missed. End of TK goal: about 15 to 20 uppercase and 12 to 16 lowercase letter names. This deck is a sample of 16, so write the uppercase and lowercase results separately in your notes. These letters are not the ones used in the earlier games. If you have those record sheets, compare them. If the child misses 4 in a row, stop and write down how many were tried. Find the Letter at the top of this stop is the part this standard is written for. The standard asks the child to match a spoken name to its printed form, and naming a letter on sight is harder than that, so rate this standard on the Find the Letter count and keep this deck as the extra note. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of any deck. A child sitting exactly at that goal still lands near 60 percent of whatever sample you show, and the suggested rating reads that as approaching. Set the rating yourself against those two counts.

title: Name the Group
dir: Help the beach friend sort things into groups. Listen to your teacher. Tell what group they belong to.
panel: Say each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Point to row 1. Say: Look at these. What group are they all in? (animals) Point to row 2. Say: What group are these in? (food, things we eat) Point to row 3. Say: Three of these are in a group. One does not belong. Which one? (watermelon) Then ask: Why? (it is food, the rest are animals) Point to row 4. Say: What group are these in? (clothes, things we wear) Accept the group word or a clear description, like things you wear. Naming single items one by one does not count as naming the group.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Big, Between, Tallest
dir: Help the beach friend look at the picture. Listen to your teacher. Use words that tell size and place.
panel: Say each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Give the student a moment to look before the first question.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Point to row 1. Say: Here are two of the same animal. Which one is big? Tell me where it is. (the one on the right, the second one) Point to row 2. Say: Where is the turtle? (between the two, in the middle) Point to row 3. Say: Which one is the tallest? (the middle one) Tell me how you know. (it is the biggest, it goes up the most) The child may point, which shows understanding, but the standard asks the child to say the word. Write down which words the child used on their own.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Sound to Letter
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter that makes the sound.
panel: Say each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Row 1. Say the sound /m/ (not the letter name). Say: Point to the letter that says /m/. (m) Row 2. Say the sound /s/. Say: Point to the letter that says /s/. (s) Row 3. Point to the beach ball. Say: Beach ball. What is the first sound? (/b/) Now point to the letter that makes that sound. (b) Row 4. Point to the sun. Say: Sun. What is the first sound? (/s/) Now point to the letter that makes that sound. (s) The letter name does not count in place of the sound. If the child says the letter name, ask: What sound does it make?Then fill in the counts below.

title: How Books Work

Say: Show me the title of this book. (the words at the top, Pip at the Beach) Picture 2 (the page). Say: Show me where I start reading. (the first word, top left, "Pip") Picture 2 again. Say: Show me with your finger which way we read. (left to right, then down to the next line) Count it as correct if the finger sweeps left to right. Picture 3. Say: One of these books is turned the wrong way. Which book is right-side up? (the one on the right)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Write My Name
dir: Get a pencil and paper. Write your name.
panel: The student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud. Then read the text on the screen aloud, once, and again if the student asks.The student works on paper. Ask to see it when they finish.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Give the child paper and a pencil. Say: Write your name on the paper. Do not spell it for them or write it in view. Look at what is on the paper. Check three things: most of the letters are there, the letters go left to right, and the first letter is a capital. Letters that are reversed or a little off do not count against the child. This standard says nearly correct. Keep the paper or take a photo for the file.Then fill in the counts below.

title: How Many, No Counting
dir: Hold the card to look. Let go to hide it. Tell how many without counting.
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Hold a card for about 2 seconds, then let go so it hides. Say: How many shells did you see? If the card does not hide on your device, cover it with your hand. Card order: 3, 5, 2, 4. Right answers: 3, 5, 2, 4. Count a correct answer as quick if the child says it without pointing or counting one by one. If the child counts each one, say: Tell me without counting. Note that the child counted.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Add and Take Away

title: Why Pines Stay Green
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about pine trees. Then answer out loud.
text: Why Pines Stay Green Most trees drop all their leaves. They do it when the cold comes. A pine tree does not. Its leaves are thin, hard needles. Each needle has a waxy coat. That coat keeps the water inside. A needle can stay on the branch. It may stay two years or more. The tree lets a few go. It drops just a few each time. So it is never bare. That is why a pine looks green. It is green in every season.
qs: What do most trees do when the cold comes?
What are a pine tree's leaves like?
What does the waxy coat on a needle do?
How long can one needle stay on the branch?
Ask me a question about pine trees.

title: Read the Story
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: A portage is one part of a trip. You carry the canoe overland from one lake to the next. Dalia had carried the canoe twice already. The trail to the second lake was long. It was longer than it had looked on the map. The canoe rode upside down on her shoulders. It sat there like a heavy wooden hat. Halfway along she set it down in the ferns. She sat on a rock to catch her breath. Then her cousin Omar came back down the trail. He took hold of the front end and lifted. With two of them under it, the canoe felt like a different boat. They walked the rest of the portage together. They slid it into the water without stopping once.

title: Warm on Top, Cold Below
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about lake water. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Warm on Top, Cold Below On a hot afternoon the top of a lake feels warm. It can feel like bath water. Your feet hang a little deeper down. They are cold. The sun only heats the first few feet of water. Warm water is lighter than cold water. So it floats and stays on top instead of mixing in. Wind stirs that top layer and spreads the warmth sideways. But the stirring does not reach very far down. In a deep lake the water near the floor can stay cold all summer long.
qs: What heats the water at the top of a lake?

title: Why Confetti Floats Down
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: Confetti is cut up paper. Paper is very light. The bits spin as they fall. The air pushes up on them. So they fall down slow. A rock would drop fast.

Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Read aloud to the student: Confetti is just paper cut into tiny bits. A sheet of paper is already light, and a tiny piece of it is lighter still. When you toss a handful up, the bits do not drop straight down. Air gets under each one and holds it, and the bit tips and spins and slides from side to side on its way down. That is why confetti seems to hang in the air. A stone the size of one of those bits would hit the ground right away, because the air cannot hold something that heavy.Say and look for: Read the six lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. title: How a Band Stays Together
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about marching bands. Then answer each question out loud.
text: How a Band Stays Together A marching band has nobody out in front waving a stick. The players are all moving. Most of them cannot see each other. So a band holds together by sound instead. The bass drum lays down a steady beat. The beat is low and loud. Every player steps on it. Sound travels about a thousand feet in one second. That seems quick. But a long band can stretch far enough. The players at the back hear the drum a little late. Good bands fix this by watching the feet ahead of them as well as listening.

title: The Squirrel and the Ribbon
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the fable. Then answer out loud.
text: The Squirrel and the Ribbon A squirrel found a long red ribbon lying on the grass after the school show. This is the finest thing in the whole wood, she said. Then she carried it up to her branch. All afternoon she wound the ribbon around and around herself. So that nobody else could take any of it. Then the wind came up the hill. The ribbon caught the wind like a sail. It pulled hard. The squirrel had to let the whole thing go. She could not keep her grip on the branch. A wren had been watching all day. She picked the ribbon up out of the grass. She wove it into her nest. There it kept three eggs warm all spring.
qs: Retell this fable in your own words. Tell what happened first, next, and last.
What is the lesson of this fable?

Tell what happened first, next, and last.Answer: A retelling with the main events in order: the squirrel finds the ribbon, she takes it up to her branch and wraps it around herself so nobody else can have any, the wind catches it and she has to let it go, and a wren takes it and builds it into a nest for her eggs. Count it correct when the big events are there in the right order, in the student's own wordsWhat is the lesson of this fable?Answer: Any sensible lesson about hoarding, such as: keeping a thing to yourself does not make it worth more, or a thing is worth more when it is used than when it is hidden away. title: Two Who Made a Difference
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about him. Answer out loud.
text: George Washington Carver was born into slavery. It was in Missouri. He was set free as a small child. He wanted to learn so badly. He walked miles to a school. That school would take him. Later he worked his way through college. He became a scientist who studied plants. Farmers near him grew cotton. They grew it year after year. Their soil wore out. Their crops failed. Carver showed them something. They could plant peanuts and sweet potatoes. That put the goodness back in the soil. Then he found hundreds of uses for those crops. So farmers could sell them. He gave his findings away free. He taught poor farmers on a wagon. He drove it from farm to farm.
